google.title: VR therapy in Hampshire: how it works and fees | Re;mind
google.description: VR therapy in Hampshire at Re;mind, Whiteley: face heights, crowds or spiders in a headset with your therapist beside you. Sessions, fees and safety.

notes.title: How the page appears on Google
notes.text: The blue title and the short description are written by us, and the search phrase comes first in both. The web address carries it too: remindmht.com/vr-therapy-hampshire/. Most people decide from these lines alone.

notes.title: The main headline
notes.text: It asks the question people type and answers it in the same line: “Where can I get VR therapy in Hampshire? At Re;mind in Whiteley”. It is the first thing anyone who lands here reads, and it tells Google plainly what the page is about.

notes.title: The opening answer
notes.text: Four short sentences answer straight away: where, what it is, how it feels, how long it takes. This is the part Google and AI assistants such as ChatGPT are most likely to quote.

notes.title: The search phrase in the section headings
notes.text: The first heading under the headline asks “What does VR therapy in Hampshire involve?” and the lines beneath answer it. The same words come back naturally in a few more headings, never stuffed in. The other headings are the questions people put to Google most: does it work, is it safe, what does it cost.

notes.title: The picture description
notes.text: Every photograph carries a short written description that Google reads and that a screen reader speaks aloud. This one carries the search phrase as well.

notes.title: Signs of experience and trust
notes.text: Written by Susie Deacon and clinically reviewed by Dr Jane Gilbert, Doctor of Clinical Psychology, with the date it was last updated, at the top of the page. Further down, the page says who delivers the sessions, with her qualifications and a client’s words from a Google review. Google is careful with health pages and favours ones that a real, qualified person stands behind.

notes.title: Honest about safety, limits and the research
notes.text: The page says plainly what the side effects are, who should talk to you first, and that VR therapy is not a cure. It names the research it draws on and links to it. Honesty of this kind reassures a worried reader, and Google and the AI assistants reward it.

notes.title: Claire’s story as proof
notes.text: Seven appointments, 169 minutes in the headset, a fear score down from 92 to 43. A client’s story answers the question “does it work?” better than any claim, and the button leads to the full case study, which links back here. Claire is an example, written to show how a real client story would look and built from published VR research; a real client’s story, shared with their permission, would take her place.

notes.title: Clear fees and a fair comparison
notes.text: What the first call, the assessment and each session cost, how many sessions a course takes, and how VR therapy compares with the alternatives. Most people want to know the cost before they call, so showing it removes a reason to leave. Anything in square brackets is our best guess for you to confirm.

notes.title: Questions and answers
notes.text: Six questions people ask about VR therapy, each answered in a few plain sentences. Clear questions with short answers are exactly what Google and AI assistants look for when someone asks a question.

notes.title: Ways to get in touch
notes.text: The form sits at the top of the page and again at the bottom, and your phone number is in the top bar of every page. Nobody has to hunt for it.

notes.title: Working quietly in the background
notes.text: Behind the scenes, the page carries labels that tell Google what it is: a service, VR therapy, offered by a therapy practice in Whiteley, with its questions and answers clearly marked for Google. The page also loads quickly on a phone and works for people who use a screen reader or larger text.
